enhanced.fullText:
The Higher Education Act's Drug and Alcohol Abuse Prevention provisions, codified at 20 U.S.C. § 1011i and implemented through 34 CFR § 86, establish comprehensive requirements for institutions of higher education to prevent illicit drug use and alcohol abuse on campus. This regulation mandates that all Title IV-eligible institutions maintain drug and alcohol abuse prevention programs and conduct biennial reviews of their effectiveness.

Under 20 U.S.C. § 1011i(a), institutions must annually distribute written materials to all students and employees describing: (1) standards of conduct prohibiting unlawful drug and alcohol possession, use, or distribution; (2) applicable legal sanctions under federal, state, and local law; (3) health risks associated with substance abuse; (4) available counseling, treatment, and rehabilitation programs; and (5) disciplinary sanctions for policy violations.

The biennial review requirement under 20 U.S.C. § 1011i(e) mandates institutions determine the number of drug and alcohol-related violations and fatalities occurring on campus or during institutional activities reported to campus officials. This review must assess program effectiveness, ensure disciplinary sanctions are consistently enforced, and identify necessary program modifications. Institutions must maintain documentation of these reviews, including statistical data on violations, fatalities, and corrective actions taken.

34 CFR § 86.100 defines the scope of coverage, applying to all students enrolled and employees working at any site where educational activities occur, including off-campus locations and study abroad programs. The regulation encompasses all controlled substances under the Controlled Substances Act (21 U.S.C. § 812) and alcohol abuse violations.

Enforcement mechanisms are stringent. Under 20 U.S.C. § 1011i(f), failure to comply results in loss of federal funding eligibility, including Title IV student financial aid programs. The Department of Education may initiate proceedings to terminate, limit, or suspend institutional participation in federal programs. Additionally, 34 CFR § 86.300 requires institutions to impose disciplinary sanctions on students and employees, which may include completion of rehabilitation programs, suspension, expulsion, or termination.

Recent enforcement actions have emphasized the importance of comprehensive documentation and meaningful biennial reviews. Institutions must demonstrate active assessment of program effectiveness rather than perfunctory compliance. The Department has clarified that reviews must include quantitative analysis of incident trends and qualitative assessment of prevention program impact.
enhanced.summary: Mandates Title IV-eligible institutions maintain drug/alcohol prevention programs, conduct biennial effectiveness reviews tracking violations and fatalities, and distribute annual policy notifications to all students and employees or face federal funding loss.
enhanced.requirements:
## Core Prevention Program Requirements
- Develop written drug and alcohol abuse prevention program per 20 U.S.C. § 1011i(a)
- Establish standards of conduct prohibiting unlawful substance possession, use, or distribution
- Implement disciplinary sanctions for policy violations as required by 34 CFR § 86.100
- Provide counseling, treatment, and rehabilitation program information

## Annual Distribution Obligations
- Distribute written materials to all enrolled students and employees
- Include applicable legal sanctions under federal, state, and local laws
- Detail health risks associated with illicit drug use and alcohol abuse
- Specify institutional disciplinary sanctions and procedures

## Biennial Review Requirements
- Conduct comprehensive program effectiveness review every two years per 20 U.S.C. § 1011i(e)
- Document number of drug and alcohol-related violations and fatalities on campus
- Assess consistency of disciplinary sanction enforcement
- Identify and implement necessary program modifications
enhanced.reportingRequirements: Biennial reviews must be completed every two years with documentation maintained on-site. Annual distribution of prevention materials required by start of each academic year. No federal submission required, but institutions must maintain comprehensive records for Department of Education audit purposes.
